name: Den Helder
title: Den Helder Ship Gauging: UTM for Offshore Vessels and Ferries
description: Ship gauging in Den Helder for offshore supply and walk-to-work vessels, Texel ferries and workboats: deck, tank and hull UTM alongside or in floating dock.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Offshore Support Ships, Ferries and Workboats in Den Helder
intro: Den Helder looks across the Marsdiep to Texel, and its harbour serves three fleets at once: the Royal Netherlands Navy at its main base, the supply and support ships working gas platforms and wind farms in the North Sea, and the ferries crossing to Texel from morning to night. Offshore vessels come alongside between campaigns and the local yard docks ferries, workboats and offshore craft, and those stays are when gauging fits in. Technicians fly in from India for each job and join the vessel at its quay or in dock.

highlights.h: Offshore ships between North Sea campaigns
highlights.p: Platform supply vessels, walk-to-work ships and rescue standby craft return to Den Helder when a contract ends or a crew rotation is due. A few days alongside allow deck, tank and crane-pedestal gauging before the next charterer's condition survey or vessel audit.

highlights.h: Texel ferries in their quieter months
highlights.p: The double-ended ro-pax ferries on the Marsdiep crossing are all needed in the summer season. Car-deck plating, ramp structure, voids and the shell where the ferries bear against their berths are best gauged when the timetable allows one ship to be released.

highlights.h: Floating docks and slipways at the yard
highlights.p: Damen Shipyards Den Helder runs floating docks and slipways for ferries, offshore support ships, tugs and workboats, and can arrange the old naval graving dock at Willemsoord for longer refits. With the hull dry, bottom shell, sea chests and stern structure are open to measurement.

port.h: The Marsdiep harbour: navy, offshore supply and the Texel crossing
p: Den Helder sits at the northern tip of the North Holland peninsula, where the Marsdiep separates the mainland from Texel and links the North Sea with the western Wadden Sea. Strong tidal streams run through the Marsdiep, so harbour movements, pilot boarding and the approach to the quays are timed with the current in mind. The town has been a naval port for centuries, and the Royal Netherlands Navy still occupies much of the waterfront from its main base, with civil shipping using the quays alongside. The Noordhollandsch Kanaal starts here and carries inland traffic south towards Alkmaar and Amsterdam, and Den Helder Airport, on the edge of town, flies helicopter crews out to offshore installations, which is one reason the town grew into an offshore logistics hub.

Commercial traffic at Den Helder is specialised rather than large. The port is a supply base for gas fields in the Dutch sector of the North Sea, so platform supply vessels, emergency response and rescue vessels, walk-to-work ships and offshore construction support craft load deck cargo, fuel, water and bulk liquids here between trips. The decommissioning of ageing gas platforms and the growth of offshore wind off the Dutch coast have widened that work. TESO's ferries shuttle between Den Helder and 't Horntje on Texel throughout the year, and fishing vessels, pilot craft, survey ships and harbour tugs make up the rest of the regular users. Deep-sea cargo ships seldom call; the port earns its living by servicing and turning around vessels that work offshore.

The rhythm of the harbour follows offshore contracts and the weather. Support ships work in rotations and come back for crew change, loading and short repairs, and because the calmer months are the busiest for construction, decommissioning and survey campaigns at sea, many offshore owners prefer to dock and survey their vessels in winter, when fewer charters are running. Ferry operators reason the same way: every ferry is needed during the Texel tourist season, so dockings and heavier maintenance tend to fall outside it. Navy maintenance periods bring their own contractors to the harbour as well. For thickness gauging this means the realistic windows are usually known well ahead and last days rather than hours, which suits structured work to a TM plan.

facilities.h: Docks, slipways and quays for gauging in Den Helder
p: Damen Shipyards Den Helder is the docking yard in the port. It operates several floating docks, the largest of which takes ships of over a hundred metres, together with open and covered slipways and a repair berth, and it can arrange the historic graving dock at Willemsoord, part of the former naval dockyard, for longer refits. Ferries, offshore support ships, workboats, tugs and government vessels pass through it, and the yard also keeps a site at Oudeschild on Texel. With a vessel in dock, the team gauges to the thickness measurement plan while the hull is dry, covering bottom and side shell, sea chests, the rudder and stern area and whichever tanks the yard has opened and ventilated.

Afloat work centres on the offshore supply quays and the berths used by the ferries and harbour craft. A support vessel alongside between contracts can usually empty and ventilate ballast, fuel and drill-water tanks over a few days, which allows proper internal gauging rather than a hurried external check. Deck plating under the cargo rails, crane and A-frame pedestals, towing and mooring fittings and the tank tops beneath deck cargo are the areas charterers question most often. Ferries are gauged at their lay berth or between sailings, depending on what the operator can release. Access to the naval base itself is restricted, and any work inside it is arranged only through the navy and its contractors.
list: Damen Shipyards Den Helder floating docks — bottom shell, sea chests, stern frame and tank gauging on ferries, offshore support ships and workboats while they are dry.
The yard's open and covered slipways — hull and internal readings on tugs, pilot boats, fishing vessels and other small craft hauled out for maintenance.
Willemsoord graving dock, arranged through the yard — refit dockings long enough for a full renewal survey programme worked alongside steel renewal.
Offshore supply quays — internal tank, deck and pedestal gauging on supply, standby and walk-to-work vessels lying alongside between charters.
Texel ferry berths — car-deck, ramp, void and shell readings on the Marsdiep ferries when one ship can be released from the timetable.

context.h: Inspectors, charterers and a changing North Sea at Den Helder
p: Port state control in Den Helder is the work of the Human Environment and Transport Inspectorate (ILT), applying the Paris MoU regime, and the same inspectorate acts as flag state for the Dutch-flagged ferries and harbour craft based here. Offshore support ships face a second audience in their charterers: gas operators and wind farm owners audit vessels before and during a contract, and a ship with gaps in its structural records or overdue tank inspections can lose work before any regulator becomes involved. Recent thickness readings, located on the TM plan and tied to the class survey history, are the evidence those audits look for.

The fleet working from Den Helder is changing with the North Sea itself. Dutch gas production is declining, so a growing share of offshore work is the decommissioning of platforms and pipelines, while offshore wind construction and maintenance keep expanding. Vessels move between those markets, often after conversions that add motion-compensated gangways, cranes or extra accommodation, and each conversion raises questions about the deck and hull structure carrying the new equipment. Ships of 500 GT and above calling at EU ports must also carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, which becomes a practical matter for older support vessels nearing the end of their working lives.

jobs.h: Gauging requests we see for Den Helder vessels
jobs.p: Most Den Helder jobs are on ships that work offshore and come home to this port, so the gauging is timed to a crew change, a gap between contracts or a docking slot at the yard rather than to a cargo call. Superintendents want two things from it: a steel picture good enough to plan renewals before the next class survey, and records that will satisfy a charterer's vessel audit. Ferry operators ask for similar work in their maintenance season, often with crack detection added at ramp hinges and car-deck supports. Scopes are agreed in advance so that tanks are emptied and ventilated before the team arrives. Typical requests:
list: A platform supply vessel between charters: deck plating under the cargo rails, drill-water and ballast tanks gauged, and crane pedestal welds checked by MPI ahead of an on-hire survey.
A walk-to-work ship after a season with a new gangway: thickness readings and crack detection on the gangway and crane foundations and the deck structure beneath them.
A Texel ferry in floating dock: bottom and side shell, sea chests, car-deck plating, ramp structure and voids gauged for the renewal survey, with steel renewal marked out.
An emergency response and rescue vessel alongside: shell plating and the hull belting along the waterline, where fender contact and corrosion combine, gauged before a docking.
A tug or workboat on the yard's slipway: shell, bottom and tank readings for an intermediate survey or a sale.

logistics: Amsterdam Schiphol is the usual arrival airport, and from there the team travels north to Den Helder by train or by road. Access to the offshore supply bases and the shipyard is controlled, and anything inside the naval area needs its own clearance, so the ship's agent or the yard registers the technicians in advance. The team comes from India on Schengen visas, which take time to issue; because contract gaps and docking slots here are usually fixed some weeks ahead, we use that notice to apply early and book travel to the confirmed date.

faqs.q: Can you gauge an offshore supply vessel during a crew change in Den Helder?
faqs.a: A short crew change leaves time only for deck and external work, such as deck plating, air pipes and pedestal welds. If the vessel stays alongside for a few days, the crew can empty and ventilate selected tanks for internal gauging as well. We plan the scope around how long the operator expects the ship to remain in port and order the work so the most important spaces are measured first.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Den Helder?
faqs.a: Yes. Damen Shipyards Den Helder operates floating docks and slipways suited to ferries, offshore support ships, workboats and tugs, and can arrange the graving dock at Willemsoord for longer jobs. Larger offshore construction ships that exceed those docks go to yards elsewhere around the North Sea, and readings taken in Den Helder before they leave can still define their steel list.

faqs.q: Does the strong current in the Marsdiep affect a gauging job?
faqs.a: Not once the vessel is secured alongside or in dock. The current matters for movements: a ship shifting from a quay into the floating dock, or arriving from offshore, waits for suitable tidal conditions, and that can move the start of a job by some hours. We stay in contact with the agent or the yard about the movement plan, so the team boards as soon as the vessel is in position.

faqs.q: Can a Texel ferry be gauged without taking it out of service?
faqs.a: Partly. Deck, ramp and some void readings can be taken while the ferry lies overnight or between sailings, if the operator allows access. A renewal survey scope that includes the shell and sea chests needs the ferry dry in the floating dock. Operators often combine the two: preliminary readings while the ship is still sailing, so the yard can plan steel, then the full programme in dock.

faqs.q: Which structural records do offshore charterers usually ask to see?
faqs.a: Vessel audits typically ask for the current class survey status, the thickness measurement report from the last renewal or intermediate survey, evidence of tank inspections and coating condition, and records of repairs to deck and crane foundations. Where those records are thin or old, owners use a condition gauging between charters in Den Helder to bring them up to date before the audit.
